alignment.note: Greek ἦραν and Latin sustulerunt are finite aorist/perfect verbs ('they took up'); the Syriac ܘܫܩܠܘ fuses the conjunction and verb into a single prefixed form, so the conjunction and verb here share one token.

Greek κλάσματα ('fragments') and Syriac ܩܨܝܐ render a single noun, whereas the Vulgate expands into a fuller phrase reliquias fragmentorum ('the remnants of the fragments'), doubling the lexical expression with reliquias as an appositional clarifier not present in the Greek.

Greek uses the genitive κοφίνων with the noun πληρώματα ('basketfuls', lit. 'fullnesses of baskets'); the Vulgate renders this attributively as cophinos plenos ('full baskets'); the Syriac employs a circumstantial clause ܟܕ ܡܠܝܢ ('while [they were] full') governing ܩܘܦܝܢܝܢ, a construction-level divergence expressing the same sense of filled baskets.

Greek uses the preposition ἀπό plus the genitive article τῶν; the Vulgate mirrors this with de; the Syriac again fuses preposition and conjunction into the prefixed ܘܡܢ, and lacks an explicit article corresponding to τῶν, typical of Syriac nominal syntax.
